newsitem.title: UK: UK says BT broadcast ban to go gradually.
newsitem.headline: UK says BT broadcast ban to go gradually.

text.p: Britain's new President of the Board of Trade, Margaret Beckett, said a broadcast ban on British Telecommunications Plc will be lifted gradually as pledged in the ruling Labour Party's election manifesto.
Beckett told a news conference on Wednesday the principle of the ban's lifting remained as promised.

But she declined to say when the lifting of the ban was expected to start, saying that would depend on when franchises had been awarded to BT's competitors and whether there was effective competition "on the ground".
She also declined to say whether the lifting of the ban would be on a regional basis.
"The general approach has always been that it would be on a rolling basis geared to when the awards of franchises for BT's competitors took place," Beckett said.
"It would not be right for the ban simply to be lifted when in some areas individual competitors' franchises have been awarded much later than in others."
But Beckett said it would also be important when deciding the timing of lifting the ban to see what BT was prepared to do to improve access to the information superhighway.

Labour's election manifesto confirmed its policy was to gradually lift restrictions on telephone companies offering entertainment services from 1998, endorsing an all-party parliamentary committee report compiled a couple of years ago.
In a promise seen at the time as a 'quid pro quo', BT promised Labour it would offer free "superhighway" computer services to schools, libraries and hospitals.

Labour added in its manifesto that it wanted full competition throughout the country, adding that it expected telecoms groups to rapidly develop the high-grade networks necessary for interactive communications across the country.

But relations between Labour and BT were strained last month by the announcement by BT chairman Sir Iain Vallance that the company would legally challenge any windfall tax on its profits imposed by the new government.

The Labour Government has said it would impose a one-off windfall tax on what it called the "excess profits" enjoyed by privatised utilities, whose fat executive salaries and surging dividend payments to shareholders have enraged consumer groups.
